pages.x: German peasants owed their lords rents, labour and fees, and the lords kept adding more, while the woods, rivers and game were closed to them. In June 1524, the story goes, the countess of Stühlingen, near the Swiss border, ordered her peasants to gather snail shells for her in the middle of the harvest. They refused, and the revolt began.

In March 1525 the peasant bands of Upper Swabia met in the town of Memmingen and agreed on Twelve Articles. They asked to choose their own pastors, to fish and hunt, and to be free of serfdom, since Christ had redeemed all people with his blood. Printed again and again, some 25,000 copies spread across Germany in two months.

The revolt spread north and east, and townsfolk and miners joined in. On Easter Day 1525 a band from the Odenwald stormed the town of Weinsberg and made Count Helfenstein and his knights run between lines of pikes to their deaths, while his wife, a daughter of the old emperor Maximilian, looked on. Lords across Germany heard of it with terror.

pages.t: The knight with the iron hand
pages.x: Götz von Berlichingen, a knight who had lost his right hand in a siege and wore one made of iron, led the Odenwald band for a month, forced to, he said later. Florian Geyer, another knight, led a Black Company of peasants. With other bands they besieged the bishop's fortress above Würzburg, and failed to take it.

In Thuringia the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer told the peasants that the end of the world was near, and that the godless lords must fall. He marched from Mühlhausen to join the peasant army under a white banner painted with a rainbow. His enemies later claimed he had promised to catch the princes' cannonballs in his sleeves.

The peasants quoted Martin Luther, who had taught that Christians were free. But Luther feared chaos more than he loved their cause. In May 1525 he wrote a pamphlet against the "murderous, thieving hordes" of peasants, urging the princes to strike them down like mad dogs. Many peasants never trusted him again.

On 15 May 1525 the princes' armies found the peasant army behind a ring of wagons on a hill above Frankenhausen. Their cannon opened fire, the peasants broke, and some 6,000 were cut down as they fled, for the loss of a handful of soldiers. Müntzer was found hiding in a house in the town, tortured and beheaded.

One by one the bands were destroyed. At Saverne in Alsace the Duke of Lorraine's men massacred peasants who had surrendered. Leaders were beheaded and villages burned and fined. The great sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider, a councillor of Würzburg who had sided with the rebels, was jailed and, it is said, tortured.

The princes won. Serfdom lasted in parts of Germany into the 1800s, and the Reformation, which had seemed to promise freedom, came under the rulers' control: they now chose their subjects' faith. But the revolt was never forgotten, and Germans from Goethe to the rulers of East Germany made heroes of its leaders.
